Stuck in the East

By: Graham Coetzer | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Having accepted job offers to teach English in China, some 50 South African youths are now the subject of a criminal investigation for working without permits, and stuck in the East

Unique Selling Point:
Some 50 South African youngsters have all been scammed by a company called SANDA Youth International. This Chinese based company has been recruiting South Africans to teach English in China. The youths were promised that SANDA Youth International would sort out all their visa and work permit requirements for an upfront fee of R8000 and a cut of the salaries they would earn in China. Most of them flew to China on student visas, and handed over their passports to SANDA personnel on arrival, ostensibly so that there work permits could be obtained. But according to the youths, in the last week SANDA director and Chinese national Owen Wang was arrested. They have been interrogated by Chinese customs officials and told they were working illegally in China. Their passports have been confiscated. And they are now stuck in China at a university in Chan Chun province. They have been told not to speak to their parents about the investigation. They have also been told that they are welcome to stay on and study at the university at their cost. The parents have contacted the SA embassy in China as well as DIRCO but have been told, on email, that there is very little that can be done for their children.

Further information:
We have asked the children to film video footage of where they are staying and the parents have sent videos, and images through. We have been given the documentation SANDA Youth International used to lure the youths and lull the parents into believing everything was above board. According to the presentations and slides it is very clear that they were offered teaching jobs in China, and that all documentation would be taken care of by the company. So the idea for the story would be to highlight the plight of the out of pocket parents and the kids who are now basically held hostage in a foreign country, and to pressure DIRCO and the SA government into getting the situation resolved. There are at least 5 parents who have agreed to do interviews, as well as their children via we chat or skype. Some of them are nervous of talking to us as they fear repercussions from the Chinese government.

Press Release:



Stuck in the East
No job, no work permit and no money to return home – that’s the nightmare facing 50 South African youths stuck in China. The group, who were individually hired by a dubious recruitment agency to teach English in the East, are now the subject of a criminal investigation after their passports were confiscated because they didn’t have legitimate visas. Their parents are desperate to get them home, but not even the South African Embassy seems to be able to help. Carte Blanche investigates.


Script:


Stuck in China
13 June 2018

Voice
According to statistics from the International Monetary Fund, China is currently ranked as the world’s second largest economy by GDP, and last year alone the Chinese Embassy in South Africa granted over 1200 work visas to South Africans seeking employment in the Far East.

Link Derek
Thousands of South African school-leavers are struggling to get a job. And when the chance came to teach English in China at a good salary, many students and their parents jumped at the opportunity.

Voice
Liza Bold is one of the mother’s of a group of about 50 South African youths who were promised teaching jobs in China, by this company, SANDA Youth International. But her daughter Lee-ann’s dream job has turned into a nightmare. She and all the other South Africans recruited by SANDA, who’ve sent us this footage, have been accused of working in China illegally, had their passports confiscated and are now stranded there.

Sound Up Liza
She was getting very depressed because she can’t find work, and she was very eager to work.

Voice
The 21 year old Lee-Ann, a qualified software developer, was impressed by SANDA director Owen Wang’s marketing pitch. Along with the adventure of working in a foreign country, Wang promised a R16 000 a month salary, which seemed a fortune considering that applicants didn’t need a BA degree or teaching qualification.

Sound Up Liza
Derek: What did they promise at this presentation?

Liza: As far as I understood, we would get a student visa on this side, they would go over, study at a university for two weeks, get to know the country, they would get their work visas, they would go to the schools and start working.

Voice
Renier Venter has played for both the Blue Bulls and Griquas under 20 rugby teams. His father Charl says the SANDA pitch convinced Renier to leave a potentially promising career as a professional rugby player to pursue his dreams of becoming a teacher.
 Sound Up Charl
My son Renier went over on the 12th of January, was approached by Owen, which is the owner of the company. And then in actual fact, a week later, he flew over to Hangzhou, where he actually worked for four months, at a school, and he was in heaven.

Voice
On arrival in China the young South Africans were told to hand over their passports to Owen Wang who said he was getting their work visas sorted. Initially they were housed in this dilapidated dorm at the Guanghua University in the city of Changchun, where living conditions left much to be desired.

Sound Up Liza
She told me how bad it was, I didn’t realise it was that bad, until I went there.

Voice
But they were soon posted to different schools around the country to start their new lives as teachers. This footage shows Charl’s son Renier in action.

Sound Up Renier and School Kids
Can you see the monkey? Yes I can.

Voice
But in April the South African’s were told to report back to the Guanghua University.

Sound Up Charl
Two months ago they had to fly back to the university in Changchun. There were some issues they had to sort or some classes they had to attend to. And the next thing we heard was immigration was pounding down the doors, confiscating visas and saying that the kids are not allowed to work in the country.

Voice
With their passports confiscated they’ve been living in limbo for the past two months, unable to earn any money to support themselves. They’re now staying in these communal dorms at the university, which while modest, are better than when they first arrived there. Demi Fourie, who is also stuck there, says they’ve been told not to leave the campus.

Sound Up Demi
I mean I’ve told my mom I might as well be in prison, it’s the same thing. I’m not allowed to do anything, I can’t go to another city, I can’t even get all of my belongings that aren’t with me. And we have no money

Sound Up Charl
Derek: Charl how much has this cost you?

Charl: You know what, up to now I’ve spent over R70 000, but the funds are running dry. You know, once you do send money, the kid is not going to sit there and eat on his own. He’s going to share his money, he’s going to share his food.

Voice
The university has offered the South Africans about R200 every week, but Charl’s son Renier says that’s not enough to get by.

Sound Up Renier
My dad has been the only person who’s been pulling me through life here, giving me money, and that’s the reason I wanted to come to China because I wanted to stop that, stop leeching from my dad, and then it just continued. There’s no way of surviving if you don’t have people sending you money.

Voice
Meanwhile, Owen Wang, who kept 50% of the youngsters salaries as commission, has disappeared off the radar. Our telephone calls and emails to him have gone unanswered. The South Africans in Changchun have been told that Wang was arrested because they were employed without work visas.

Sound Up Liza
They said that he’s been arrested, but we don’t know how true that is.



Voice
The Chinese Embassy in South Africa declined to comment on an ongoing investigation, but in a written response warned South Africans “to carefully read the Exit and Entry Administration Law of the People’s Republic of China and Rules for the Administration of Employment of Foreigners in China to fully understand how to work legally in China”. The SA Department of International Relations and Cooperation’ spokesperson Ndivhuwo Mabaya says the matter has been escalated to minister Lindiwe Sisulu, who is negotiating with her Chinese counterpart on behalf of the South Africans.

Sound Up Mabaya
Derek: What is the latest situation, when can we expect these students to fly home?

Mabaya: I wish I could give you a date. We will not be able to give you a date, but I can tell you this matter is now receiving the highest attention. Our minister has now written to the foreign minister, and we want to make sure that their passports are released.

Voice
The minister will need to count on the strong diplomatic relationship between South Africa and China to further the cause, because the reality is the South African government cannot legally interfere with another country’s sovereignty.

Link Derek
It’s not just the students who ended up in a visa minefield in China. Madri van den Heever had a degree and work permit, and landed up behind bars.

Voice
Unlike the students who fell for SANDA’s empty promises, van den Heever was offered a job directly from a school in Beijing, and obtained a working visa to do so herself when she, husband Ettienne and baby boy Benji set off for China.

Sound Up Madri
Everyday was a fantastic experience. Working with the children, going to school, we were all very very happy there.

Voice
But on the 24th of April this year, the carefree family’s world came crashing down around them. Van den Heever was arrested because her work visa specified the wrong campus of the school she worked for.

Sound Up Madri
Madri: So I was employed at the Chaoyang campus, while my visa was for a campus in Daxing.

Voice
But she says the worst was not knowing when she would be released to see her husband and child again

Sound Up Madri
I didn’t know if they were ok, Benji has never been away from me for a single day. I think that is the worst punishment for any mother, is to be taken away from your child.

Voice
After 15 sleepless nights, Van den Heever was taken to the airport and told she was being deported.

Sound Up Madri
It was very sad seeing Ettienne, because he was very emotional. And Ettienne is not an emotional guy. Ettienne is not an emotional guy, he is a happy chappy. He’s always happy, always full of jokes. And it was really hard to see him like that.

Voice
Having been deported from the country, van den Heever will not be allowed to visit mainland China again for the next five years. In the SANDA case, if the South Africans do get their passports back, they’ll have to rely on relatives to foot the bill for their airfare.

Sound Up Mabaya
Derek: What can you do once this is sorted out and they’ve got the passports, to fly them back home because many can’t afford it?

Mabaya: Under normal circumstances, we don’t fly people home. And this is one of the things South Africans must know. But we can bring this case to the attention of the minister, I think it’s something that we can look at, and we might be able to find a way to deal with it.

Voice
For the families back home, that day can’t come soon enough.

Sound Up Liza
Liza:It’s very hard.

Derek: I really am sorry it’s just such an unnecessary thing.

Liza: I just want my child back.

So the idea for the story would be to highlight the plight of the out of pocket parents and the kids who are now basically held hostage in a foreign country, and to pressure DIRCO and the SA government into getting the situation resolved. There are at least 5 parents who have agreed to do interviews, as well as their children via we chat or skype. Some of them are nervous of talking to us as they fear repercussions from the Chinese government.
